abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Urbanization reshapes ecological interactions at the human–animal interface, yet how it structures viral diversity in urban avian communities remains unclear. Here, we present a pan‐urban viromic analysis of avian samples collected across 22 cities in China. We identified 52,314 viral operational taxonomic units, broadly representing species‐level viral clusters, revealing extensive and previously underexplored viral diversity. Viral richness varied markedly among cities, largely reflecting variation in bacteriophage diversity, whereas vertebrate‐associated viruses showed a comparatively narrower diversity range. Network analyses revealed pronounced geographic structuring of avian viromes, with several cities sharing viral lineages with multiple other cities and acting as hubs of virome connectivity, linked by a core set of widely distributed viral families alongside substantial local heterogeneity. Sequence similarity and phylogenetic analyses showed that 63.1% (2994/4746) of vertebrate‐associated viral sequences shared less than 80% similarity with their closest known references, including 65.6% (2718/4143) of DNA virus sequences and 45.8% (276/603) of RNA virus sequences, highlighting pervasive viral novelty across genome types. Further comparisons with reference sequences identified candidate associations with diverse annotated host taxa, including mammals and humans. Functional profiling of auxiliary metabolic genes revealed a highly skewed repertoire dominated by CysH (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase), a key enzyme in assimilatory sulfate reduction, suggesting that phages may modulate sulfur assimilation in infected bacterial hosts and potentially influence sulfur metabolism in urban bird‐associated microbial communities. Together, these findings provide a nationwide view of the spatial organization, evolutionary diversity, and cross‐host association patterns of viruses in urban birds, highlighting their role in shaping viral ecology in human‐dominated environments.

Urban birds share habitats with humans and other animals, yet their viromes remain poorly characterized. Metagenomic profiling of 985 fecal samples from 22 Chinese cities identified 52,314 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs; 17,439 eukaryotic and 34,875 phage). Among 4746 sequences, 63.1% showed <80% similarity to their closest references. Across cities, these viromes showed shared lineages and local variation, with phage‐associated vOTU richness spanning a wider observed range than vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic vOTU richness. Sequence comparisons found human‐associated matches in 16 genera and 105 close matches involving 57 reference‐annotated host taxa. Auxiliary metabolic gene annotations included 264 contig‐Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) Orthology pairs in 34 categories, dominated by CysH (phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase), suggesting sulfur assimilation potential. These findings expand the urban avian virome catalog for One Health surveillance.

list-item.p: Urban avian communities harbor extensive and underexplored viral diversity across China.

Urban avian viromes showed strong geographic structuring shaped by shared and local viral lineages, whereas phage richness varied more widely across cities than vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic viral richness.
Sequence‐based cross‐host associations highlight the potential value of urban bird fecal viromes for surveillance.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Birds are characterized by exceptional species diversity and complex patterns of habitat use and migration, rendering them major natural reservoirs for a wide range of viruses and key drivers in the evolution, emergence, and dissemination of novel viral lineages [1]. In recent years, the intensification of human activities has increasingly blurred the boundaries between wildlife, livestock, and human populations, leading to more frequent contacts at the human‐animal interface. Such interconnected human, animal, and environmental systems are increasingly viewed within a One Health framework [2]. Under these conditions, viruses harbored in birds may gain opportunities to overcome species barriers, giving rise to potential zoonotic risks to human health [3]. Avian influenza viruses exemplify this broader risk because they pose persistent threats to both poultry production and public health and can cause severe disease in humans, with some strains having adapted for efficient transmission among human populations [4].

Advances in high‐throughput sequencing and metagenomic approaches have greatly expanded the capacity for pathogen detection and viral discovery [5]. Over the past decade, an increasing number of studies have investigated avian‐associated viruses and uncovered a substantial amount of previously underrecognized viral dark matter, including viruses from diverse groups such as astroviruses, picornaviruses, caliciviruses, parvoviruses, retroviruses, adenoviruses, and CRESS‐DNA viruses, as well as an unexpectedly high abundance of bacteriophages, many of which show low sequence similarity to known viruses, thereby expanding our understanding of the distribution patterns and overall diversity of viruses harbored by birds [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. In parallel, targeted surveillance of viruses of major public health relevance has demonstrated the role of migratory wild birds in the long‐distance dissemination of H5N8 avian influenza virus [11], revealed how avian migration and recombination shape the transmission and diversity of gamma‐ and deltacoronaviruses [12], and characterized the prevalence, host distribution, and genetic diversity of coronaviruses in Australian wild birds through regional polymerase chain reaction (PCR)‐based surveillance [13]. Collectively, these pathogen‐focused studies have provided critical insights into the occurrence, evolution, and transmission of specific high‐risk viruses. However, their focus on predefined viral groups does not resolve the broader taxonomic composition, community‐level organization, or spatial structure of avian‐associated viromes. Among untargeted metagenomic surveys, Shan et al. analyzed 3182 birds from eight provinces in China using 215 pooled libraries, providing broad insights into viral diversity across host groups and geographic regions [6]. More broadly, existing datasets either relied on pooled libraries organized by host species and sampling location [6, 8] or focused on a single region, clinical cohort, or isolated ecological system [7, 9, 10]. These design features have limited standardized comparisons at the individual‐sample level and constrained inference on the large‐scale spatial organization of avian‐associated viromes.

Urban environments constitute highly heterogeneous and interconnected ecosystems in which human activities profoundly influence wildlife community structure, host contact patterns, and opportunities for pathogen transmission. Urban‐adapted wildlife, represented by birds and rodents, have been widely documented as key components of zoonotic disease systems; for example, rodent‐associated pathogens such as plague [14], leptospirosis [15], and hantaviruses [16] have been linked to urban ecological contexts. In birds, an important group of synanthropic hosts, the effects of urbanization on pathogen transmission and evolution are particularly evident. Avian exposure to mosquito‐borne West Nile virus has been shown to increase with the intensity of urbanization [17], while proximity to human habitation is associated with greater diversity of bacterial pathogen lineages and antimicrobial resistance determinants in wild bird populations [3]. These effects may operate differently across the major components of the avian virome. Phages may respond indirectly to changes in their bacterial host communities [18], whereas vertebrate‐associated viruses may be influenced by avian host movement and exposure at urban animal‐human interfaces [8, 19]. At a broader ecological level, urbanization may shape avian viral ecology and potential spillover risk through four interconnected pathways. First, habitat loss and fragmentation alter the size and composition of urban habitat patches, thereby reorganizing bird assemblages [20] and potentially modifying host densities and contact networks relevant to viral circulation. Second, urbanization can increase opportunities for contact between humans and wild birds [3], while anthropogenic food and water resources may also increase spatial overlap between wild birds and domestic animals [21], creating opportunities for pathogen exchange at human‐animal interfaces. Third, ecological interactions between birds and other vertebrates may provide additional opportunities for viral sharing. Birds may prey on bats and other small vertebrates [22], while birds and bats can also share roosting or nesting sites [23], creating direct or environmentally mediated interfaces between avian and mammalian hosts. Fourth, migratory movements connect geographically distant bird populations and can facilitate the long‐distance dissemination and genetic exchange of avian viruses [11, 12]. Together, these processes indicate that ongoing urbanization and landscape transformation modify ecological connectivity and host‐pathogen interactions, thereby altering transmission dynamics and increasing opportunities for pathogen spread, including viral transmission and cross‐species spillover, within human‐dominated environments. Despite growing recognition of these effects, avian viromes have rarely been compared across multiple cities using individual‐sample data generated under a common experimental and analytical framework. A geographically broad pan‐urban perspective is therefore needed to resolve the spatial organization of these viral communities across urban systems. Such a design enables standardized inter‐city comparisons, distinguishes broadly distributed viral components from locally structured variation, and reveals large‐scale patterns of virome connectivity that may remain obscured in single region or pooled sample studies.

Here, we present a pan‐urban viromic analysis of avian samples collected from densely populated urban areas across China. By integrating individual‐sample metagenomic sequencing with a common comparative framework, we characterize viral diversity and composition across cities and evaluate the spatial organization, connectivity, and potential cross‐host associations of urban avian viromes.

sec.title: Large‐scale survey of the urban avian virome
sec.p: To investigate the large‐scale organization of the urban avian virome across China, we analyzed bird fecal samples collected from diverse urban environments between 2024 and 2025 (see Methods). In total, 985 samples were obtained from 22 cities spanning 18 provincial‐level administrative regions, with sampling conducted in densely populated areas within each city (Figure 1A). These samples consisted of freshly deposited bird droppings collected from vehicle windshields, providing a non‐invasive snapshot of viral material detected in bird‐derived fecal samples. Avian hosts were inferred using mitochondrial marker genes (e.g., cytochrome c oxidase subunit I [COI], cytochrome b [cytb], and NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 [ND2]) detected in the fecal material, indicating representation from approximately 22 avian orders, with Passeriformes predominating across most locations (Table S1). Among these libraries, 255 were assigned with high confidence at the species level based on concordant matches of two independent mitochondrial marker genes (Table S2).

sec.p: To estimate the number of viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs) represented by the viruses identified in this study, including eukaryotic viruses and bacteriophages (phages), we clustered the viral sequences at 95% average nucleotide identity (ANI) with an alignment fraction of 85% relative to the shorter sequence. This yielded 52,314 vOTUs, representing species‐level clusters. Among all vOTUs, those assessed by CheckV as Medium‐quality, High‐quality, and Complete accounted for 33.2% of the total. The vOTU representatives had a median genome length of 4381 bp, and 6355 vOTU representatives exceeded 10 kbp in length. As shown in Figure 1B, a clear truncation is observed in the genome length distribution, reflecting the inclusion of manually curated shorter eukaryotic viral genomes in the CheckV assessment. Building on this, we applied the framework described by Nayfach et al. [24] to further group species‐level vOTUs into higher taxonomic ranks (genus and family) based on pairwise average amino acid identity (AAI) and gene‐sharing patterns. This analysis yielded 13,702 genus‐level vOTUs and 4238 family‐level vOTUs. Rarefaction analyses relating the number of libraries to the accumulation of vOTUs indicated that, when all vOTUs were included, viral taxa at the species, genus, and family levels had not yet reached saturation (Figure 1C). This pattern was primarily driven by the large proportion of rare vOTUs represented by a single sequence. By contrast, restricting the analysis to vOTUs composed of at least two conspecific viral sequences resulted in rarefaction curves that approached saturation at the genus and family levels.

Across cities, vOTU richness showed pronounced variation among avian host orders and geographic regions (Figure 1D). Passeriformes consistently showed high vOTU richness across most sampled cities, suggesting a broadly distributed, virus‐rich host group at the national scale. In contrast, Columbiformes, Psittaciformes, Galliformes, and Charadriiformes were detected across many cities, but vOTU richness was generally lower and less widespread than that observed in Passeriformes. To assess whether this inter‐city variation was associated with broad‐scale geographic separation, we conducted city‐level distance‐based analyses. Neither the absolute difference in standardized total viral richness (Mantel Spearman ρ = 0.032, p = 0.789, q = 0.789) nor Bray–Curtis dissimilarity (ρ = 0.248, p = 0.0432, q = 0.0864) varied significantly with pairwise great‐circle distance (Table S3). Standardized total viral richness was also unrelated to latitude (ρ = 0.081, p = 0.713) or longitude (ρ = 0.028, p = 0.907), indicating no significant geographic structuring of inter‐city viral richness at the spatial scale examined in this study. Under the opportunistic and spatially heterogeneous framework of urban sampling, vOTU richness exhibited substantial variability across cities, precluding straightforward links to simple large‐scale spatial variables. At the same time, the absence of such broad‐scale associations does not rule out the presence of more structured patterns at finer ecological scales, including those related to virus sharing among co‐occurring bird populations within urban environments.

sec.title: Urban patterns of vertebrate‐ and phage‐associated viruses
sec.p: Detected vOTU richness varied by ~15‐fold across the 22 sampled cities (Figure 2A). Cities with the lowest vOTU richness, including Shanghai (663 vOTUs), Xianyang (774 vOTUs), Aral (846 vOTUs), and Nyingchi (866 vOTUs), were characterized by a predominance of vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic vOTUs. In contrast, cities with higher vOTU richness showed an increasing contribution of phage‐associated vOTUs, which dominated the virome composition in cities with the highest richness, such as Guangzhou (9905 vOTUs) and Zhenjiang (10,380 vOTUs). Phage‐associated vOTUs spanned a much broader richness range across cities (139–8249 vOTUs) than eukaryotic vOTUs, whose richness remained comparatively constrained (median, 931 vOTUs; IQR, 618–1352; maximum, 3045). Differences in sampling intensity and local sampling conditions among cities may have contributed to the observed inter‐city variation in total vOTU richness. To summarize the overall taxonomic composition of the detected vOTUs, we examined their distribution at the family level. The detected vOTUs comprised 34,875 phage‐associated vOTUs and 17,439 vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic vOTUs. Among phage‐associated vOTUs, Unclassified Caudoviricetes was the most abundant group (n = 21,744), followed by Microviridae (n = 11,707), together accounting for the majority of phage‐associated viral diversity. In contrast, vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic vOTUs were less diverse at the family level, with Parvoviridae representing the most abundant family (n = 7604). Here, eukaryotic vOTUs were categorized as putatively vertebrate‐associated based on the documented host range of their assigned viral families, as described by ICTV taxonomy and previous studies (https://ictv.global/report).

sec.p: We next tested whether the measured four‐indicator urbanization gradient accounted for the observed inter‐city virome differentiation. The composite index was not associated with sampling‐standardized richness for all viruses (Spearman ρ = −0.096, p = 0.675), phages (ρ = −0.110, p = 0.631), or vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic viruses (ρ = 0.034, p = 0.887). It also did not explain community composition by PERMANOVA (all viruses: R 2 = 0.054, p = 0.146; phages: R 2 = 0.055, p = 0.186; vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic viruses: R 2 = 0.054, p = 0.191). Multivariate environmental distance was not correlated with Bray–Curtis dissimilarity for any viral group (Mantel ρ = 0.025, 0.031, and −0.009, respectively; all p > 0.806), and none of the individual indicator‐richness associations was significant after false discovery rate correction (all q = 0.979; Table S4).

To assess the abundance patterns of vertebrate‐associated viruses, quality‐controlled reads from each metagenome were mapped to the corresponding vOTU representatives to calculate vOTU‐level relative abundances in fecal samples. A total of 32 vertebrate‐associated eukaryotic viral families were identified, including 15 RNA virus families and 17 DNA virus families (Figure 2B). Among the 32 families, Parvoviridae was the most prevalent, occurring in 932 and 911 libraries at reads per kilobase per million mapped reads (RPKM) > 0 and >0.1, respectively, corresponding to a detection rate of 94.6% at RPKM > 0. To distinguish frequent detection from broad and even spatial distribution, we quantified family‐level occupancy, dominance, and distribution breadth across cities and avian orders. Parvoviridae, Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Picornaviridae were classified as pan‐urban ubiquitous. All four families were detected in all 22 cities and in 16–21 of the 22 assigned avian orders, with low city‐level Berger–Parker dominance values (0.066–0.118) and high standardized Levins breadth values (0.659–0.923), indicating broad and relatively even distributions. In comparison, Astroviridae, Anelloviridae, Coronaviridae, and Adenoviridae were detected in 19–21 cities but showed less even spatial distributions and were classified as widespread but uneven. The 13 geographically restricted families exhibited two distinct patterns. Tobaniviridae and Orthoherpesviridae were each detected in only one city, whereas Rhabdoviridae and Smacoviridae were detected in 14 and 16 cities, respectively, but were strongly concentrated in Xi'an and Chifeng, with city‐level dominance values of 0.551 and 0.785, respectively. LEfSe analysis identified 16 high‐effect city‐associated viral signatures with q values < 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction and LDA scores > 4.0. Among these, Rhabdoviridae was enriched in Xi'an (q = 2.36 × 10−43; LDA = 5.063) and differed significantly from all other cities. Smacoviridae was enriched in Chifeng (q = 9.56 × 10−36; LDA = 4.623) and differed significantly from most other cities (Table S5).

Subsequently, we compared the composition of vertebrate‐associated viral communities across avian orders to characterize the taxonomic structure of the avian virome. Average virus carriage profiles were calculated at the family level for each avian order, and pairwise similarity among orders was assessed using Bray–Curtis similarity [25]. Hierarchical clustering grouped the orders into five clusters (Figure 2C). To examine whether this clustering was associated with host evolutionary relatedness, we compared pairwise phylogenetic distances among the avian orders with their Bray‐Curtis virome dissimilarities. Host phylogenetic distance was not significantly associated with virome dissimilarity (Mantel‐type Spearman ρ = −0.107 to −0.091, p = 0.762–0.817), with sensitivity analyses yielding consistent results (Table S6). Among the viral families contributing to these clustering patterns, Parvoviridae, Genomoviridae, Rhabdoviridae, Circoviridae, and Picornaviridae were the most influential. The highest similarity was observed between Falconiformes and Galliformes (similarity = 0.851), followed by Accipitriformes and Passeriformes (0.842), Accipitriformes and Columbiformes (0.833), Falconiformes and Passeriformes (0.825), and Galliformes and Passeriformes (0.821). In contrast, substantially lower similarities were observed for several order pairs involving Psittaciformes, including Galliformes (0.545), Falconiformes (0.575), Passeriformes (0.655), Charadriiformes (0.657), and Accipitriformes (0.680). Consistent with these results, similarity‐based network analysis further indicated that, although Passeriformes (n = 552) and Columbiformes (n = 224) were represented by the largest sample sizes in this study, their associated virome compositions remained distinguishable (similarity = 0.805). Passeriformes occupied a highly connected position in the similarity network, sharing similar virome compositions with multiple avian orders. In contrast, Columbiformes exhibited a more restricted connectivity pattern, showing high similarity primarily with Accipitriformes (0.833). In addition, Psittaciformes consistently exhibited low similarity to all other avian orders.

sec.title: Geographic structuring of shared vertebrate‐associated viromes
sec.p: To further characterize the spatial similarity of avian vertebrate‐associated viromes across geographic regions, a vOTU‐based geographic similarity network was constructed, revealing clear patterns of virome sharing among sampling sites (Figure 3A). After retaining candidate site pairs whose observed Jaccard similarity exceeded the pooled 99th percentile of the permutation null distribution and additionally requiring a Jaccard similarity ≥0.06 with at least 30 shared vOTUs, edges were predominantly concentrated in central, eastern, and northeastern China, where sampling sites formed dense clusters. In contrast, sampling sites in northwestern China and several other regions exhibited substantially fewer connections. Overall, clear differences in vOTU sharing were also observed between southern and northern China, together resulting in an uneven spatial distribution of virome similarity.

sec.p: From a network perspective, sampling cities differed markedly in both the number and strength of their connections, indicating pronounced geographic structuring of avian viromes. Several cities, including Beijing, Xi'an, Harbin, and Wuhan, formed similarity links with multiple other sampling sites and occupied relatively central positions in the network. Xi'an and Beijing were each connected to at least seven other cities, involving 1104 and 944 shared vOTUs, respectively, while Harbin shared 1019 vOTUs across connections with six other cities. In contrast, several cities had few or no retained connections. Ürümqi was linked to relatively few cities but showed comparatively strong sharing with particular regions, suggesting a localized association pattern. To quantify these patterns, we calculated normalized degree, weighted betweenness, and weighted closeness centrality for each city in the thresholded vertebrate virome‐sharing network. Cities were classified as hubs when at least two of the three centrality metrics were in the upper quartile and as peripheral when at least two metrics were in the lower quartile (see Methods). Beijing, Xi'an, Harbin, Shanghai, Wuhan, and Tai'an met the hub criterion. Beijing and Xi'an had the highest degree centrality values (0.333 each) and betweenness centrality values of 0.152 and 0.105, with closeness centrality values of 0.0324 and 0.0306, respectively. Harbin and Wuhan also showed relatively high degree centrality (0.286 and 0.238) and closeness centrality (0.0288 and 0.0268), whereas Shanghai and Tai'an satisfied the hub criterion based on their combined centrality profiles. Nine isolated cities were classified as peripheral, while Chengdu, Nanjing, and Ürümqi were classified as intermediate (Table S7).

Within the virome similarity network, we compared the family‐level composition of shared and unique vOTUs at the site level (Figure 3B). For each focal site, shared vOTUs represented the union of vOTUs shared with significantly connected partner sites, whereas unique vOTUs were restricted to that site across all sampling locations. Overall, shared vOTUs differed in taxonomic composition from unique vOTUs across most sampling sites. Shared vOTUs were consistently dominated by a limited number of viral families, most prominently Parvoviridae, Circoviridae, and Genomoviridae, which together constituted a substantial proportion of the shared vOTU pool in highly connected sites such as Harbin, Beijing, Xi'an, and Wuhan. These families contributed considerable numbers of vOTUs across geographically distant sites, suggesting the presence of broadly distributed viral lineages that contribute to inter‐site virome similarity. In contrast, unique vOTUs displayed a more heterogeneous and site‐specific family composition. Although several families abundant among shared vOTUs were also detected in the unique fraction, unique vOTUs showed a broader representation of lower‐abundance families and a greater contribution of site‐restricted viral families. This pattern was particularly evident in sites such as Ürümqi, Yinchuan, and Chengdu, where unique vOTUs exceeded shared vOTUs and encompassed a wide range of viral families. Across sites, the balance between shared and unique vOTUs varied. Highly connected sites tended to harbor larger pools of shared vOTUs dominated by a small number of widely distributed viral families, whereas more peripheral or weakly connected sites were enriched for unique vOTUs with diverse family affiliations. Together, these results suggest that inter‐city virome connectivity is primarily shaped by a core group of widely distributed viral families, while locally restricted viral diversity contributes substantially to site‐specific virome composition.

sec.title: Diversification and evolution of viruses in urban birds
sec.p: To further characterize the evolutionary composition of urban bird viromes, we next assessed the phylogenetic relationships and sequence divergence of the detected viral lineages. A total of 4746 viral sequences were included for phylogenetic reconstruction (Figure 4), spanning 19 viral families and the phylum Cressdnaviricota; sequence information is provided in Table S8. Phylogenies were inferred using amino acid sequences of the RNA‐dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) for RNA viruses and non‐structural proteins, including replicase, for DNA viruses. For Anelloviridae and Papillomaviridae, nucleotide sequences of ORF1 and L1, respectively, were used, following ICTV recommendations. BLAST‐based similarity analyses revealed extensive genetic divergence among the detected viral sequences. Overall, 2994 sequences (63.1%) shared <80% similarity with their closest references. Within the genome‐type subsets, 2718 of 4143 vertebrate DNA virus sequences (65.6%) and 276 of 603 vertebrate RNA virus sequences (45.8%) met this criterion. This divergence varied markedly across viral families. Coronaviridae exhibited uniformly high similarity (100%, 39/39 ≥ 80%), consistent with relatively conserved or well‐represented lineages. In contrast, several DNA virus families showed substantially lower similarity. Only 6.25% (1/16) of Papillomaviridae sequences exceeded 80% similarity, whereas 81.44% (1817/2231) of Parvoviridae and 76.92% (40/52) of Polyomaviridae sequences fell below this threshold. Notably, Cressdnaviricota and Parvoviridae were the most abundant viral groups identified in this study, likely reflecting combined contributions from dietary input, environmental exposure, and the intrinsic diversity of the avian gut virome.

caption.p: Phylogenetic trees of 19 viral families and Cressdnaviricota. Viruses identified in this study are highlighted with red branches, and their sequence identity to the best matches in public databases is indicated on the right side of each tree. Detailed information for all viral sequences generated in this study is provided in Table S8. Phylogenetic trees were primarily constructed based on amino acid sequences of the RNA‐dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) for RNA viruses and the replicase and other non‐structural proteins for DNA viruses. In accordance with ICTV classification guidelines, the phylogenetic tree for Anelloviridae was reconstructed using nucleotide sequences of ORF1, whereas the phylogeny of Papillomaviridae was inferred using nucleotide sequences of the L1 ORF.

sec.p: Specifically, 141 viral sequences belonging to the family Anelloviridae were identified. Phylogenetic analysis showed that 17 of these sequences exhibited substantial genetic divergence from all currently recognized genera. Although their closest relatives were members of the genus Thetatorquevirus, these sequences formed a well‐supported and distinct lineage clearly separated from existing taxa, and thus likely represent a distinct subgenus‐level lineage. In addition, 39 coronavirus genomes were identified, including 15 assigned to Gammacoronavirus and 24 to Deltacoronavirus. These sequences showed high similarity to their closest references (97.8–99.7%), including Gammacoronavirus galli, avian gammacoronavirus, Deltacoronavirus lonchurae, Deltacoronavirus HNU1‐2, and Sparrow coronavirus HKU17. Eight Deltacoronavirus sequences detected in birds from multiple regions (Shandong, Ningxia, Shaanxi, Qinghai, and Xinjiang) were also identified in drinking water samples collected from live poultry markets in Jining City, Shandong [26], suggesting a potential environmental transmission route. Recombination analyses of all 39 coronavirus genomes using RDP5 [27] and SimPlot [28] did not identify any clear or consistently supported recombination signals. Furthermore, 16 viral sequences belonging to the family Papillomaviridae were identified, including 15 assigned to Etapapillomavirus and one to Lambdapapillomavirus. The Etapapillomavirus sequences were associated with avian hosts but showed substantial genetic divergence from previously reported avian lineages. In contrast, the single Lambdapapillomavirus sequence exhibited high similarity (99.6%) to a feline papillomavirus previously identified in a domestic cat with cutaneous papillomatosis [29]. The detection of a feline‐associated papillomavirus in bird‐derived samples represents an unexpected host association signal, although incidental environmental contamination from shared urban surfaces cannot be excluded. The detected Picornaviridae‐related sequences were predominantly associated with avian picornaviruses (e.g., Megrivirus, Passerivirus, and Hepatovirus), consistent with their origin in the avian gastrointestinal tract. A smaller fraction of sequences was related to invertebrate‐ and plant‐associated picorna‐like viruses, likely reflecting trophic interactions and environmental inputs.

Notably, a subset of sequences also showed high similarity to known animal‐associated viruses. These included duck parvoviruses (59.5–97.2% amino acid identity), avian adenoviruses (61.7–99.7%), and sequences related to avian hepatitis E viruses (81.8–82.1%). In addition, multiple sequences were affiliated with Astroviridae and Caliciviridae, indicating the presence of enteric viruses with potential cross‐host associations. One Mamastrovirus‐related sequence shared 93.9–95.3% amino acid identity with viruses previously detected in swine fecal samples from China, Vietnam, and India, suggesting a potential link between avian‐associated viromes and swine enteric viruses. Similarly, goat torovirus was independently identified in two samples from Xinjiang, sharing 97.6% and 99.5% amino acid identity with reference sequences. Members of Sedoreoviridae were also identified, including sequences related to Rotavirus A (94.6–98.9%), which has been reported in both avian and mammalian hosts, and Rotavirus G (95.9–98.9%), which has been detected in both wild birds and domestic poultry (e.g., chickens). Collectively, these findings suggest that urban birds may contribute to the maintenance and dissemination of viruses of veterinary importance across host boundaries.

sec.title: Sequence similarity associations with reference‐annotated hosts
sec.p: To assess host association patterns, we focused on viruses assigned to known viral genera based on high‐confidence BLASTn matches (≥90% nucleotide identity and ≥80% query coverage) [30]. These thresholds were used to identify viral sequences showing close genetic relatedness to known references. The top five hits were retained for each query sequence, and host information was assigned based on the annotated host information of the corresponding reference sequences (Table S9).

A total of 45 known viral genera from 19 viral families were retained to construct the network of viruses and reference‐annotated hosts, covering 80 host species distributed across 19 orders and 7 classes (Figure 5, Figure S1, Figure S2). Based on host annotations from the BLASTn hits, 17 genera were linked to two or more host species, among which 13 were further associated with multiple host orders, whereas the remaining genera were linked to a single host species or order. Several genera exhibited broad inferred host association patterns. Gemycircularvirus showed the broadest reference‐annotation coverage (23 host species across 11 orders), followed by Gemykibivirus (12 species across 8 orders), Circovirus (6 species across 5 orders), Protoambidensovirus (21 species across 4 orders), and Bocaparvovirus (9 species across 3 orders), suggesting broad inferred host associations across taxonomic levels.

sec.p: Based on BLASTn matches to reference sequences annotated as human‐associated, a total of 16 viral genera were represented among the matched sequences. These reference sequences were derived from diverse sample types, including vaginal, nasopharyngeal, blood, fecal, and oral metagenomes. Viruses related to the family Anelloviridae predominated, including Alphatorquevirus (n = 40), Betatorquevirus (n = 17), and Gammatorquevirus (n = 10) (Figure S3). Values in parentheses represent the number of query sequences assigned to each viral genus based on BLASTn matches. In addition, Torbevirus (n = 22), a member of the family Redondoviridae, was also highly represented, with associated reference sequences primarily derived from respiratory tract and oral cavity samples. Additional genera were identified at lower frequencies, including Deltapolyomavirus, Gemykibivirus, and Orthopicobirnavirus (each n = 3), as well as Cyclovirus, Galvornvirus, and Iteradensovirus (each n = 2), whereas the remaining genera (e.g., Betapolyomavirus, Gemygorvirus, Gemyvongvirus, Orthorubulavirus, Protoparvovirus, and Sadetorquevirus) were each represented by a single match. Quantitative profiling further showed that these viral lineages were generally infrequent and geographically unevenly distributed (Table S10). Torbevirus was the most frequently detected genus, occurring in 53 of 985 libraries (5.4%) across 5 of 22 cities, with a mean RPKM of 2757.4 across all libraries. This was followed by Alphatorquevirus, detected in 22 libraries (2.2%) across 4 cities (mean RPKM, 1076.6), and Orthopicobirnavirus, detected in 17 libraries (1.7%) across 4 cities (mean RPKM, 647.1). Notably, Torbevirus showed marked geographic heterogeneity, with the highest prevalence observed in Chifeng (37.5%), Guangzhou (35.0%), and Haikou (25.0%). In contrast, each of the remaining 13 genera was detected in no more than 1.4% of libraries. Together, these results indicate that although Anelloviridae‐related taxa accounted for the greatest number of identified viral sequences, their distribution across individual libraries was limited, whereas Torbevirus showed the broadest and most frequent detection among the human‐associated viral genera.

Candidate associations with reference‐annotated host taxa were identified from BLASTn matches with ≥99% nucleotide identity and ≥80% query coverage were observed across different host species. Based on these criteria, 136 associations were retained, involving 105 viral sequences and 57 annotated host taxa (Figure S4). Of these, 24 viral sequences were linked to two or more host taxa, whereas the remaining 81 matched references annotated with a single host taxon. The maximum number of reference‐annotated host taxa linked to a single query sequence was four. The network included both viruses assigned to known genera and those lacking genus‐level classification, with multiple reference–host taxa represented in both groups. Host annotations were dominated by mammals, with additional links to other vertebrate and invertebrate taxa. A subset of query sequences matched human‐associated references, most belonging to the single reference–host taxon group. Only one Paramyxoviridae‐related sequence (XJ_2221_247) matched references annotated with humans and the genera Equus and Sus. This sequence was detected in a single library in this study and showed elevated relative abundance (RPKM = 1804.87), ranking 14th among 54 vertebrate‐associated viruses identified in that library.

We further performed model‐based zoonotic prioritization of the detected viral sequences using the zoonotic_rank [31] framework (Table S11). Viral sequences were stratified into priority categories according to their model‐predicted scores. Sequences matching multiple reference–host taxa were enriched among higher‐scoring candidates (Very high and High categories; 18/24), whereas sequences matching a single reference–host taxon were predominantly distributed across lower and intermediate score ranges (Figure S5). Notably, the Paramyxoviridae‐related sequence was predicted to pose a medium zoonotic risk. In contrast, ZJ_2336_9667 (Chaphamaparvovirus) was the only sequence matching multiple reference–host taxa and assigned a very high predicted zoonotic risk. It was detected in eight samples from Zhenjiang, suggesting a localized occurrence in this region. Members of this genus have recently been reported in a wide range of vertebrate hosts, including cats [32], dogs [33], chickens [34], and bats [35], and have been associated with diarrheal symptoms.

To evaluate whether these candidate signals were spatially concentrated, we quantified the city‐level distributions of the sequences matching multiple reference–host taxa, sequences assigned to the Very high or High zoonotic_rank categories, and the subset meeting both criteria. The resulting surveillance priority score ranked Yinchuan, Zhenjiang, Ürümqi, and Guangzhou in the first four positions. However, global spatial autocorrelation was not significant for standardized multi‐host richness (Moran's I = −0.015, p = 0.763), predicted high risk richness (I = −0.066, p = 0.854), or dual priority richness (I = −0.071, p = 0.831; all BH q = 0.854). No city remained a significant local Getis‐Ord Gi* hot spot after within‐outcome BH correction, and analyses using three‐ and five‐nearest neighbor graphs gave the same qualitative conclusion (Table S12 and Figure S6).

sec.title: Nationwide patterns of auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs) in urban birds
sec.p: To assess the metabolic functions potentially carried by phages, AMG‐like genes were screened across the vOTUs. A total of 3403 contig‐KEGG Orthology (KO) annotations were obtained from the combined VIBRANT and DRAM‐v predictions, yielding 1807 non‐redundant contig‐KO pairs corresponding to 126 distinct KOs. Following conservative curation, 264 high‐confidence contig‐KO associations were retained, reducing the functional repertoire to 34 unique KOs. Functional representation of the retained AMGs was strongly skewed, with a small subset of KOs accounting for the majority of observations. Notably, K00390 overwhelmingly dominated the retained AMG repertoire, far exceeding all other KOs in frequency (Table S13). Consequently, the overall annotated functional profile of AMGs was largely shaped by this single KO, with most annotations concentrated in a limited number of major metabolic categories, particularly those related to energy metabolism.

Across hosts, the curated AMG repertoire was distributed within a restricted set of functional categories, including energy metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins (Figure 6A). Among these, energy metabolism comprised the largest fraction, whereas the other categories were represented by fewer KOs. Several KOs were detected across multiple host groups, indicating partial overlap in AMG functional composition. AMGs were detected in 266 of 985 libraries (27.0%). Detection frequency differed among the 22 cities (Pearson's χ 2 = 330.33, df = 21, p = 2.05 × 10−57), with 123 of 231 city pairs significant after BH correction of two‐sided Fisher exact tests (q < 0.05; Table S14). Guangzhou had a higher detection frequency than Shanghai (37/40 vs. 3/40; q = 2.81 × 10−14). Among the positive libraries from 20 cities, AMG abundance differed in the omnibus Kruskal–Wallis test (H = 40.14, df = 19, p = 0.00314; permutation p = 0.00134), but none of the 190 Dunn pairwise comparisons remained significant after correction (all q ≥ 0.0623). Detection frequencies and positive‐library abundance distributions are shown separately in Figure 6B. Across cities, the proportion of AMG‐positive libraries was strongly associated with mean background phage richness (Spearman ρ = 0.867, q < 0.0001). However, mean annotated AMG gene density per Mbp of detected phage sequence was not significantly associated with mean background phage richness across the 22 cities (ρ = 0.306, q = 0.187). Among positive libraries, gene density differed among cities (H = 81.45, df = 19, p = 1.04 × 10−9), and its within‐city rank association with background phage richness was negative (r = −0.603, permutation q = 2.00 × 10−5; Table S14). No significant association was detected between AMG occurrence and any of the measured urbanization variables (all q ≥ 0.887).
