sec.p: AMGs putatively encoding phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase (CysH; KO: K00390) constituted the dominant annotated AMG signal, accounting for a large fraction of total AMG abundance. As a key enzyme in assimilatory sulfate reduction, CysH catalyzes the conversion of phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate (PAPS) to sulfite, thereby providing reduced sulfur for the biosynthesis of cysteine and methionine. This predominance identifies sulfur metabolism as the principal annotated functional signal in urban bird fecal viromes. Viral CysH genes have been reported across diverse environments, including closed‐basin lakes [36], hydrothermal vents [37], cold seeps [38], and oceanic trenches [39], indicating that phage‐encoded CysH is distributed across diverse ecosystems. Phylogenetic analysis of CysH amino acid sequences revealed that most sequences identified in this study clustered with phage‐derived homologs, forming a well‐supported clade distinct from bacterial counterparts (Figure 6C), suggesting a shared evolutionary background within viral lineages.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Urban environments represent increasingly interconnected ecological systems in which wildlife, humans, and environmental reservoirs are brought into close and dynamic contact [40]. In this context, our pan‐urban analysis reveals that avian viromes are not randomly distributed across cities but instead exhibit a structured organization characterized by a shared connectivity backbone alongside pronounced local heterogeneity. A limited set of widely distributed viral families contributed disproportionately to inter‐city virome similarity, whereas a large fraction of viral diversity remained site‐restricted. This pattern suggests that urban viromes are shaped by both widespread viral lineages and locally constrained ecological processes, providing a conceptual framework for their large‐scale organization.

A striking feature of the observed patterns is that inter‐city variation in viral richness was largely associated with phage diversity, whereas vertebrate‐associated viruses exhibited a comparatively constrained diversity range. This contrast may reflect differences in ecological drivers. Phages are closely linked to microbial communities in the avian gut and surrounding environments, which are highly responsive to local ecological conditions, including diet [41], habitat use [42], and anthropogenic influences [43]. Such context‐dependent dynamics may generate substantial variability in phage diversity across cities. Host phylogeny and host range may also contribute to the narrower observed range of vertebrate‐associated viral richness, although these potential explanations require further investigation. In this context, standardized metagenomic workflows and reproducible statistical frameworks may facilitate more consistent comparisons of viral and microbial community patterns across studies [44, 45, 46].

At the network level, the identification of highly connected cities highlights the presence of hub‐like structures within the urban virome landscape. These cities were linked to multiple regions through shared viral lineages, suggesting that they may play a disproportionate role in shaping large‐scale virome connectivity. Such patterns may arise from a combination of ecological and anthropogenic processes, including bird movement, overlapping urban habitats, and indirect environmental mixing mediated by human activities. Rather than forming isolated units, urban ecosystems appear to be interconnected through uneven viral exchange, with connectivity concentrated in specific regions.

Our analyses identified candidate associations between viral sequences detected in bird‐derived fecal samples and references annotated from diverse taxa, including mammals and humans. Although these patterns do not establish direct transmission pathways, they identify candidate cross‐host viral associations that warrant further investigation in urban environments. Birds, as highly mobile and widely distributed urban wildlife, may contribute to this process by acting as connectors across ecological niches [23]. The detection of viral sequences with high similarity across distinct host taxa, including a subset of viruses shared among multiple hosts and potentially associated with increased zoonotic risk, underscores the importance of considering urban wildlife within the broader context of cross‐host viral associations. These findings support a tiered, evidence‐informed surveillance strategy. Highly connected cities, including Beijing, Xi'an, Harbin, and Wuhan, could be prioritized as candidate sentinel sites for longitudinal monitoring of inter‐city virome connectivity. Surveillance at these locations should include repeated seasonal sampling of urban birds and paired sampling of environmental water and domestic animals. Targeted PCR and complete genome recovery would help distinguish persistent local circulation from sporadic or environmentally derived detection. Advances in Nanopore long‐read sequencing and standardized metagenomic workflows may further improve taxonomic resolution and support rapid virome profiling in future surveillance [47, 48, 49]. Preventive measures should focus on sites with frequent bird‐human or bird‐domestic animal contact, including high‐density bird congregation sites and relevant water‐access points, through improved sanitation, reduction of fecal contamination, and physical measures limiting bird access. Veterinary or public health follow‐up should be guided by repeated detection and close genomic confirmation. Molecularly confirmed abnormal signals could then be referred through existing wildlife disease information channels to forestry, veterinary, and disease‐control authorities for joint assessment and incorporated as nonclinical animal or environmental inputs into the national multi‐trigger infectious disease surveillance and early warning framework.

In addition to taxonomic and ecological patterns, functional profiling revealed a strongly biased repertoire of putative phage‐associated AMGs, dominated by sequences annotated as CysH, a phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase associated with assimilatory sulfate reduction. This pattern demonstrates the prevalence of CysH‐like sequences in the annotated dataset and indicates genomic potential related to sulfur assimilation. Viral CysH homologs have been reported across diverse environments [50], supporting the idea that phage‐mediated modulation of sulfur metabolism represents a widespread and potentially conserved ecological strategy [51]. Notably, phylogenetic analysis showed that most CysH amino acid sequences identified in this study clustered with phage‐derived homologs rather than with bacterial counterparts, consistent with their putative viral affiliation. Transcriptomic, proteomic, or experimental validation will be required to determine whether these genes are expressed and functionally active under relevant biological conditions. Inter‐city differences in AMG detection may partly reflect variation in the amount of phage sequence recovered. Although AMG occurrence was strongly associated with background phage richness, length‐normalized AMG gene density showed no significant positive association with phage richness at the city level.

In addition, several patterns at the regional and host levels are worth noting. Passeriformes were detected in all regions except Yining. Beyond potential sampling bias, this distribution pattern may reflect the relatively distinct ecological setting of the Ili River Valley in western China, where grassland and agro‐pastoral landscapes predominate. Compared with the highly urbanized regions of eastern China, differences in avian community structure and habitat use in this region may underlie the observed pattern. Notably, Yining, as the northwesternmost city included in this study, may further amplify the influence of regional ecological differences on avian community composition. At the host level, Psittaciformes consistently exhibited low similarity to all other avian orders, despite a moderate sample size (n = 50). This pattern may be driven by differences in ecological niche and dietary preferences, which may influence exposure to distinct viral communities and limit overlap with other avian groups.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. Temporal coverage was uneven among cities, which may have influenced comparisons of virome composition across locations. Although all samples were collected within the overall November 2024 to January 2025 period, individual cities were not necessarily sampled on the same dates, and the number of sampling occasions and overall temporal span were not standardized across cities. Climatic conditions also differed substantially among regions during this period. For example, winter environmental conditions in Harbin differed markedly from those in Haikou. Such temporal and climatic heterogeneity may have affected local avian activity, migration status, community composition, diet, and viral occurrence, as well as the preservation and detectability of viral nucleic acids in fecal samples. In addition, potential pseudoreplication cannot be fully excluded because multiple droppings collected from the same location during the same sampling period may have originated from the same individual, flock, or communal roost. Host identification based on mitochondrial markers and reference databases may introduce uncertainty in assigning samples to specific avian taxa and, by itself, cannot establish whether the detected avian DNA originated from wild, feral, captive, escaped, environmental, or dietary sources. In addition, detection of a viral sequence in a bird‐derived fecal sample does not demonstrate that the inferred bird was infected, because the viral nucleic acids may also derive from dietary contents, environmental contamination, or transient passage through the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, sequence similarity to host‐annotated references indicates close genetic relatedness but cannot establish host range, resolve transmission directionality, or confirm active infection. The broad reference‐annotation coverage of some viral genera may also partly reflect the diversity and availability of host‐associated reference records in current databases. Although relatively high RPKM values were also observed for other human‐reference‐associated viral genera in separate sequencing runs, and some genera were detected across multiple runs, contamination during sample processing or sequencing cannot be excluded. The detection of these sequences, including Torbevirus and Alphatorquevirus, may reflect biological or environmental sources, technical contamination, or a combination of these factors, and requires independent validation. Despite these constraints, the large‐scale and comparative design of this study provides a robust foundation for identifying broad ecological patterns in urban viromes, with fecal samples serving as a valuable proxy for assessing viromes at the interface of ecological and public health processes.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: This study provides a nationwide view of the spatial organization, evolutionary diversity, and cross‐host association patterns of avian viromes across urban China. The extensive viral diversity, pronounced geographic structuring, and detection of candidate cross‐host viral signals highlight urban birds as an important component of the human–animal interface. Although sequence‐based associations alone cannot establish active infection or transmission, they provide useful signals for identifying viral lineages and locations that warrant further investigation. Together, our findings support the value of incorporating urban bird virome surveillance into broader One Health surveillance frameworks and provide a basis for targeted longitudinal monitoring, molecular validation, and early identification of viral signals with potential public health relevance.

sec.title: Study design and sample collection
sec.p: Between November 2024 and January 2025, sampling was conducted across 22 cities in 18 provincial‐level administrative regions of China. In each city, sampling areas were selected in densely populated locations characterized by nearby green spaces and frequent bird activity, including residential communities, commercial districts, university campuses, and public parking areas. Within each sampling area, vehicles parked overnight were selected, and fresh bird droppings deposited during nocturnal roosting or flight were collected from windshield surfaces. Samples were visually inspected to ensure consistency with the typical appearance of avian feces and were collected only when a single, well‐defined fecal deposit was present without visible surrounding contamination, to minimize potential mixing from multiple individuals. To ensure sample freshness, vehicles were verified by trained field personnel to have been parked since the previous evening, and long‐term stationary vehicles were excluded to avoid older droppings. Designated field personnel conducted sampling during the study period, with fresh fecal samples collected whenever available at the selected sampling locations. Sample collection did not require direct contact with birds and was therefore non‐invasive. All samples were collected in the early morning (06:00–08:00) to minimize environmental exposure and degradation. A total of 985 samples were collected, stored in sterile containers, and transported on dry ice for subsequent processing.

sec.title: Sample processing and quality control
sec.p: All sample processing was conducted in a biosafety level 2 (BSL‐2) laboratory in accordance with standard biosafety procedures. Prior to viral metagenomic analysis, samples were mechanically homogenized under cryogenic conditions and resuspended in 0.5 mL of Dulbecco's phosphate‐buffered saline. The suspensions were vigorously vortexed for 5 min and then subjected to three freeze‐thaw cycles to facilitate the release of viral particles. Subsequently, the samples were incubated at 4°C for 30 min. After centrifugation at 15,000 × g for 10 min, the clarified supernatants were transferred to 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes and stored at −80°C until further analysis [52]. For each library corresponding to a single individual sample, the supernatant was carefully transferred into fresh 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes. The samples were then centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 5 min at 4°C, followed by filtration through a 0.45 µm membrane to enrich viral particles. The resulting filtrates were subsequently treated with RNase and DNase at 37°C for 60 min to remove unprotected nucleic acids. Total nucleic acids were extracted using the QIAamp MinElute Virus Spin Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The extracted nucleic acids, including both viral DNA and RNA, were reverse‐transcribed using SuperScript III reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen) with 100 pmol of random hexamer primers. This step was followed by second‐strand DNA synthesis using Klenow fragment polymerase (New England BioLabs). Sequencing libraries were constructed with the Nextera XT DNA Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina), and paired‐end sequencing (150 bp) with combinatorial dual indexing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Demultiplexing was performed using BCL Convert (Illumina) with one index mismatch allowed.

Throughout the experimental procedures, strict measures were implemented to prevent cross‐contamination and nucleic acid degradation. Aerosol‐resistant filter tips were used to reduce the risk of sample cross‐contamination. All consumables that came into direct contact with nucleic acid samples, including microcentrifuge tubes and pipette tips, were certified DNase‐ and RNase‐free. Samples were resuspended in DEPC‐treated water supplemented with RNase inhibitors. As negative controls, sterile ddH2O was processed in parallel under the same experimental conditions. Sample integrity and quality were evaluated using agarose gel electrophoresis and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. Control libraries yielded 242,940–2,047,790 reads and 91–982 assembled contigs per library. Taxonomic annotation of control‐derived contigs identified viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic sequences. The annotated viral families included Iflaviridae, Parvoviridae, Retroviridae, Dicistroviridae, and Picobirnaviridae, among others. Control‐associated viral sequences, together with sequences identified as potential laboratory contaminants during viral identification or previously reported as potential contaminants in the literature, were excluded from downstream analyses.

sec.title: Viral contig assembly and identification
sec.p: Primers and low‐quality reads were trimmed using fastp (v1.0.1) [53] with the following parameters: ‐q 25 ‐u 35 ‐y ‐Y 45 ‐c −3 ‐l 50 ‐‐detect_adapter_for_pe ‐g ‐x. The paired‐end reads were assembled using MEGAHIT (v1.2.9) [54] with the parameter ‐‐min‐contig‐len 500.

The viral origin of assembled contigs was determined through a multi‐step screening and refinement process. Briefly, contigs were first searched against a locally compiled non‐redundant (nr) protein database (updated on 2025‐08‐20). Contigs preliminarily classified as eukaryotic viruses were further manually curated and assembled in Geneious Prime (v2024.0.5). The curated contigs were then inspected and used as reference sequences for read mapping against the raw sequencing data using default recommended parameters, enabling the recovery of complete or near‐complete viral genomes. The resulting genomic sequences were examined for potential vector contamination using the VecScreen tool provided by NCBI. Open reading frames (ORFs) were predicted in Geneious Prime by specifying a minimum length of 100 bp and ATG as the start codon. The predicted ORFs were evaluated by sequence similarity searches against viral sequences in the GenBank database. Annotation of ORFs was performed based on conserved domain matches using the Conserved Domain Database [55].

Phage contigs were identified through a multi‐tool validation framework. Initially, contigs were screened using VirSorter2 (v2.2.4) [56] with the parameter ‐‐min‐score 0.5, followed by analysis with CheckV (v1.0.1) [57] to perform quality control of the VirSorter2 outputs and to trim potential host‐derived regions remaining at the ends of proviral contigs. Candidate phage contigs were evaluated based on outputs from VirSorter2 and CheckV, taking into account the numbers of viral and host genes, VirSorter2 viral scores, and the presence of hallmark genes. These sequences were further assessed using VIBRANT (v1.2.1) [58] with the ‐virome option and independently validated with geNomad (v1.7.4) [59]. Only contigs consistently classified as viral by these complementary approaches were retained as bona fide phage sequences.

Viral sequences were clustered into species‐level viral taxa at 95% ANI across 85% of the length of the shorter contig, in accordance with MIUViG standards [60], using a custom script from the CheckV repository. The resulting vOTUs were compared against the NCBI nr protein database using DIAMOND BLASTx (v2.1.13) [61]. Significant matches were retained using an E‐value cutoff of <10−5. Taxonomic annotation of viral sequences was performed using TaxonKit (v0.20.0) [62]. Phage sequences that could not be assigned based on similarity to known viruses were further classified using PhaGCN2 [63], in accordance with the ICTV 2024 taxonomy release.

Additionally, to minimize potential contamination, sequences suspected to originate from reagent‐ or laboratory‐derived sources were manually curated and removed to the greatest extent possible, including previously reported contaminant‐associated viruses such as CRESS‐DNA and parvo‐like hybrid viruses [64, 65, 66]. Specifically, sequences showing similarity to viral entries previously reported as common metagenomic contaminants, including those cataloged in ParvoDB [65], were excluded from further analysis, resulting in the removal of 1632 vOTUs.

sec.title: Estimating relative abundance of vOTU representatives in metagenomes
sec.p: The RPKM values were used to represent the relative abundances of viral sequences in fecal metagenomic samples and were estimated using CoverM (v0.7.0) [67]. Viral vOTU representative sequences were used to build the mapping index with BWA (v0.7.17‐r1188) [68]. Quality‐controlled reads from each sample were then mapped to the vOTU representatives using CoverM with the options ‐‐methods rpkm, ‐‐min‐read‐aligned‐percent 95, ‐‐min‐read‐percent‐identity 90, and ‐‐min‐covered‐fraction 75 to retain high‐quality mappings. Reads with sequence identity below 90% were excluded during the mapping process, and a vOTU was considered present in a sample only if at least 75% of its length was covered by mapped reads. The resulting RPKM values of vOTU representatives within each metagenome were normalized by the total RPKM to calculate relative abundance percentages [69].

sec.title: Clustering of viral sequences into higher‐rank taxonomic units
sec.p: Species‐level vOTU representative genomes were further clustered at the genus and family ranks using scripts developed by Nayfach et al. [24], incorporating gene‐sharing profiles and AAI. ORFs were predicted from vOTU representatives with Prodigal (v2.6.3) [70] using the ‐p meta option. All viral proteins were compared using BLASTp implemented in DIAMOND with the parameters ‐‐evalue 1e‐5 ‐‐max‐target‐seqs 10000. For each genome pair, protein matches with an E‐value < 10−5 were retained to calculate both the fraction of shared genes and the corresponding AAI. At the family level, genomes sharing ≥10% of genes or at least 8 genes, together with a minimum AAI of 20% (parameters: ‐min_percent_shared 10, ‐min_num_shared 8, ‐min_aai 20), were grouped and clustered using the Markov Cluster Algorithm (MCL) (v14‐137) with an inflation value of 1.2. For genus‐level classification, genome pairs sharing ≥20% of genes or at least 16 genes and an AAI ≥40% (parameters: ‐min_percent_shared 20, ‐min_num_shared 16, ‐min_aai 40) were clustered using MCL with an inflation factor of 2.0.

sec.title: Inference of avian host associations from fecal samples
sec.p: Avian host inference was conducted using mitochondrial marker genes detected in fecal metagenomic contigs, including cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI), cytochrome b (cytb), and NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 (ND2), with primary emphasis on the COI barcode gene [71]. Putative mitochondrial contigs were identified by BLASTn searches against public reference databases, including the Barcode of Life Data System (BOLD) and GenBank (E‐value ≤ 1e‐5). For each library, candidate hits were ranked by bit score, and the best match was determined primarily based on the highest bit score. When the bit score difference between the top two hits exceeded 100, the hit with the highest bit score was selected. When the difference was ≤50, nucleotide identity was used as an additional criterion. For intermediate cases (bit score difference of 50–100), nucleotide identity was prioritized when the identity difference exceeded 5%; otherwise, the hit with the higher bit score was retained. Host taxa were assigned using predefined sequence similarity thresholds. Species‐level assignments applied a ≥98% similarity threshold following mitochondrial DNA barcoding practices [71], whereas genus‐ and family‐level classifications were inferred using progressively lower operational thresholds (92–97.9% and 85–91.9%, respectively). Order‐level classification followed the lineage of the best‐matching reference sequence. Contigs lacking confident avian mitochondrial matches were excluded. Given the complexity of fecal material and the potential presence of environmental DNA or dietary residues, host inference at finer taxonomic levels may be uncertain. Therefore, downstream analyses were conservatively restricted to the order level to minimize host misassignment.

sec.title: Geographic distance analyses
sec.p: Geographic coordinates were assigned at the city level for the 22 sampling cities. Pairwise great‐circle distances were calculated using the Haversine formula and a mean Earth radius of 6371 km. Because city sample sizes ranged from 33 to 81 libraries, total viral richness was standardized to 33 libraries per city using the exact incidence‐based expectation under sampling without replacement. City‐level community profiles were calculated by normalizing vOTU RPKM values within each library and averaging the profiles of non‐zero‐sum libraries within each city; Bray–Curtis dissimilarities were then calculated between city profiles. Geographic distance was compared with the absolute pairwise difference in standardized total viral richness and with Bray–Curtis dissimilarity using two‐sided Mantel‐type Spearman tests with 5000 city‐label permutations. As a sensitivity analysis, the richness test was repeated using absolute pairwise differences in log1p‐transformed standardized richness. Associations of latitude and longitude with standardized richness were examined using exploratory Spearman tests with 5000 permutations. Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction was applied across the two prespecified geographic distance tests.

sec.title: City‐level richness and urbanization indicators
sec.p: Analyses were conducted for the 21 cities with complete urban environmental data. Nyingchi was excluded because comparable environmental indicators were unavailable. Total expected vOTU richness was standardized to a common sampling effort of 33 libraries per city. The urbanization composite comprised built‐up surface, population density, the share of built‐up surface in high‐greenness areas, and road‐network density (GHS‐UCDB R2024A). Built‐up surface, population density, and road‐network density were log1p‐transformed, the high‐greenness indicator was sign‐reversed, and all four indicators were z‐standardized across cities before averaging.

sec.title: Viral occupancy and dominance analyses
sec.p:
For each library, vOTU RPKM values were summed within each of the 32 vertebrate‐associated viral families and divided by the total vertebrate‐associated viral RPKM to obtain family‐level relative abundance. City‐ and avian‐order‐level profiles were calculated as the mean library‐level relative abundance within each group; libraries without an assigned avian order were excluded from analyses across avian orders. For each family, occupancy was calculated as the fraction of 22 cities or 22 assigned avian orders with at least one detection (RPKM > 0). Let p
i denote the share of the family‐specific profile in city or order i. Simpson concentration (D = ∑p
i
2), Berger–Parker dominance (max[p
i ]), and standardized Levins breadth (B_A = [(1/D) − 1]/(n − 1), where n is the number of cities or assigned avian orders) were calculated. Families were descriptively classified as pan‐urban ubiquitous within the surveyed network when city occupancy was ≥75%, city B_A was ≥0.50, and avian‐order occupancy was ≥50%; as geographically restricted when city occupancy was ≤25% or city Berger–Parker dominance was ≥0.50; as widespread but uneven when city occupancy was ≥75% without meeting the ubiquitous criteria; and as intermediate otherwise.

sec.title: Identification of city‐associated viral signatures
sec.p: Family‐level relative abundance profiles were analyzed using LEfSe (v1.1.2) [72]. Features were screened using the Kruskal–Wallis test with an alpha threshold of 0.05, followed by LDA effect size estimation using 5000 bootstrap iterations and an LDA threshold of 2.0. Kruskal–Wallis p values across the 32 viral families were adjusted using the BH procedure. Families with a BH‐adjusted q value < 0.05 and an LDA score > 4.0 were defined as high effect city‐associated viral signatures. For each signature, the enriched city was compared with the other cities using two‐sided Mann–Whitney U tests, with p values adjusted using the BH procedure.

sec.title: Host phylogeny‐virome association analysis
sec.p: An avian timetree was obtained from the TimeTree database (timetree.org) and pruned to the seven host orders represented in the Bray–Curtis comparison. Pairwise patristic distances were calculated from the retained branch lengths. Virome dissimilarity was defined as the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between each pair of host orders. The association between the host phylogenetic‐distance matrix and the virome‐dissimilarity matrix was evaluated using an exact label‐permutation Mantel‐type Spearman test, with all possible permutations of host‐order labels enumerated. Because the tree retrieved from TimeTree contained eight tips labeled as Charadriiformes, the analysis was repeated separately using Charadriiformes−1 through Charadriiformes−8. Pearson Mantel correlations and “leave‐one‐order‐out” analyses were additionally performed as sensitivity checks.

sec.title: Spatial similarity network and topological analysis of the city network
sec.p: For the spatial similarity network, binary Jaccard similarity was calculated from the site‐level vOTU presence‐absence matrix. For each site, the four sites with the highest observed similarity were selected as candidate partners, after which duplicate undirected pairs were removed. In each of 9999 permutations, the presence‐absence vector of each vOTU was independently shuffled across the 22 sampling sites. This preserved the overall number of sites occupied by each vOTU while randomizing the identities of the sites at which it occurred. Site‐level vOTU richness was not preserved. Pairwise Jaccard similarities were recalculated for each permuted matrix. Because the permutation was performed on the aggregated site‐level matrix, city library number, bird species richness, and host composition were not explicitly constrained or adjusted. Candidate edges were retained when their observed Jaccard similarity exceeded the pooled 99th percentile of the permuted pairwise similarities and additionally met Jaccard similarity ≥0.06 and at least 30 shared vOTUs.

In a complementary topological analysis used to classify city network roles, the number of shared vOTUs and Jaccard similarity were calculated for every city pair. Edges were retained at an empirical p value < 0.01 based on 5000 random overlap null models that preserved the vOTU richness of the two cities, together with the requirements of Jaccard similarity ≥0.06 and at least 30 shared vOTUs. Degree centrality was calculated as k/(n − 1). For weighted shortest path analyses, edge length was defined as the inverse of Jaccard similarity, and normalized betweenness and closeness centralities were subsequently calculated. Cities with at least two of the three centrality metrics in the upper quartile were classified as hubs, those with at least two metrics in the lower quartile were classified as peripheral, and the remaining cities were classified as intermediate.

sec.title: Phylogenetic analysis
sec.p: To elucidate phylogenetic relationships, sequences belonging to different groups of related viruses were downloaded from the GenBank database, along with sequences of proposed species pending ratification. Nucleotide or protein sequences were aligned using MUSCLE (v5.3) [73], and the results were trimmed with trimAl [74]. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using IQ‐TREE v2.3.6 [75], with 1000 bootstrap replicates (‐bb 1000) and the ModelFinder function (‐m MFP). Interactive Tree Of Life (iTOL) was used to visualize and edit phylogenetic trees [76].

sec.title: Sequence similarity associations with reference‐annotated hosts
sec.p: Viruses of concern were defined as viral sequences showing high similarity to viruses previously associated with humans or other hosts based on BLASTn searches (E‐value < 10−5, ≥90% nucleotide identity, and ≥80% query coverage). Host classification, isolation source, and other relevant metadata were manually curated from GenBank accession records and associated literature. Candidate reference–host associations were defined by query‐to‐reference matches with ≥99% nucleotide identity and ≥80% query coverage.

sec.title: Spatial analysis of reference‐annotation groups and predicted high risk viral signals
sec.p: We evaluated city‐level spatial concentration for the sequences matching multiple reference–host taxa, sequences classified as Very high or High by zoonotic_rank, and the overlap between these two groups. Sequence identifiers were normalized and matched to the vertebrate virus RPKM matrix before calculating city‐level metrics. A sequence was considered detected in a library when RPKM > 0. Spatial relationships were represented by a symmetric binary four nearest neighbor graph based on great‐circle distance. Global Moran's I and local Getis‐Ord Gi* statistics (including the focal city in the local statistic) were assessed using 99,999 label permutations. BH correction was applied across the three global tests and separately across the 22 local tests for each outcome.

sec.title: Identification and curation of auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs)
sec.p: AMGs were identified using a combination of VIBRANT and DRAM‐v (v1.4.6) [77]. AMGs predicted by VIBRANT in previous analyses were directly retrieved and used for downstream curation without re‐running the pipeline. In parallel, DRAM‐v was used for AMG annotation. Viral contigs were first processed using VirSorter2 with the “‐‐prep‐for‐dramv” option, and the resulting files were used as input for DRAM‐v. Candidate AMGs were assigned auxiliary scores based on the genomic context of flanking genes, and only those with auxiliary scores <4 were retained [78, 79]. The AMG candidates predicted by the two pipelines were then combined for subsequent analyses.

To improve the reliability of AMG identification and reduce false‐positive assignments, manual curation was performed following recent recommendations for AMG analysis [80]. Genes associated with core viral functions or commonly misannotated categories were excluded, including those involved in DNA replication and repair, nucleotide metabolism [81], and transcription or translation processes, as well as ribosomal proteins. In addition, genes related to viral infection and structural functions were removed, including glycoside hydrolases and peptidases involved in host cell wall degradation, as well as structural or capsid proteins. Genes involved in modification of viral components (e.g., glycosyltransferases, methyltransferases, and adenylyltransferases), and those previously suggested to represent essential viral functions rather than AMGs (e.g., dcm and queuosine biosynthesis genes, queCDEF), were also excluded. Finally, genes specific to eukaryotic cellular processes were removed. Next, the curated AMGs were grouped into KEGG orthologs (KOs) for downstream community‐level analyses. KO abundances were determined by summing the abundances of AMGs assigned to each KO. Detection was defined as total AMG abundance >0 and compared across all 985 libraries in 22 cities using a Pearson chi‐square test; all 231 city pairs were compared using two‐sided Fisher exact tests with BH correction. Detection‐rate intervals were calculated using the 95% Wilson method. Abundance comparisons included only the 266 positive libraries in 20 cities and used a tie‐corrected Kruskal–Wallis test followed by 190 Dunn comparisons with a separate BH correction. For sequence length normalization, the distinct retained AMG gene identifiers were mapped to parent phage vOTUs. For each library, we counted these annotated genes on detected phage vOTUs (RPKM > 0) and divided by the summed length of all detected phage vOTUs in Mbp. Background phage richness excluded the 246 AMG‐carrier vOTUs. Normalized correlations were assessed both within cities and between cities: within‐city analyses correlated globally ranked variables after centering ranks within each city and permuted response ranks within cities; between‐city analyses used Spearman correlations of city means or positive‐library medians, the latter restricted to cities with at least three positive libraries. Two‐sided permutation p values used 99,999 permutations and the plus‐one correction, with BH correction across the eight normalized correlation tests. Normalized gene density among positive libraries was also compared using Kruskal–Wallis and 190 Dunn tests with separate BH correction.

sec.title: Statistics and reproducibility
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using R (v4.3.3) and custom Python scripts, which are available on GitHub at https://github.com/lux9612/urban-bird-virome. Data processing and visualization were conducted using packages including dplyr, tidyverse, ggplot2, pheatmap, igraph, and ggraph, while ecological and diversity analyses were performed using the vegan package. Species accumulation curves were computed using the specaccum() function in the vegan package with the random method and 1000 permutations. Analyses were conducted at species‐, genus‐, and family‐level resolutions, with additional stratification based on cluster size (≥2 sequences). Community similarity was assessed using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity (for abundance‐based analyses) and Jaccard similarity (for presence–absence data), implemented in vegdist(). Pairwise similarity matrices were further used for hierarchical clustering and network construction. For bird order‐level comparisons, mean abundance profiles (centroids) were calculated prior to distance estimation. Network analyses were performed using igraph, tidygraph, and ggraph. Edges were retained based on similarity thresholds (e.g., top 25% quantile or predefined cutoffs), and network connectivity was ensured using a maximum spanning tree. For spatial networks, statistical significance of similarity was evaluated using permutation‐based null models (n = 9999), and edges were retained only when exceeding the 99th percentile of the null distribution, combined with additional constraints on shared vOTU counts and similarity values. No parametric assumptions were imposed unless explicitly stated. Random processes (e.g., accumulation curves, null model permutations) were controlled using fixed random seeds to ensure reproducibility. Detailed analytical parameters and settings are provided in the corresponding scripts. All data processing steps, including filtering, normalization, and transformation, were performed using scripted and version‐controlled workflows.
